title: Reverse Integer
description: Brute force to optimized: string reversal and reparse versus peeling off digits with pure arithmetic and an incremental overflow check.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a signed 32 bit integer x, reverse the order of its digits. If the reversed number falls outside the range a signed 32 bit integer can hold, return 0 instead.

blocks.text: Given a signed 32 bit integer x, reverse the order of its digits. If the reversed number falls outside the range a signed 32 bit integer can hold, return 0 instead.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Number Backwards Off a Ticket
blocks.text: Picture a numbered ticket read backwards, digit by digit, ignoring the minus sign until the very end if there is one. The tricky part is that the ticket booth only accepts numbers up to a certain size, so if the backwards reading turns out to be too large, or too negative, to fit, it has to be rejected entirely.

blocks.caption: Reverse the digits, but reject the result if it does not fit in a signed 32 bit integer

blocks.text: 321 fits comfortably in a signed 32 bit integer, so the answer is 321.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Reverse the digits","9646324351"],["Does it fit in a signed 32 bit integer?","No, it is far larger than 2147483647"]]}

blocks.text: Since the reversed number overflows the allowed range, the answer is 0.

Reversing digits sounds like a text manipulation task, but it is worth checking how much of it can be reframed as pure arithmetic instead, and what that reframing means for handling overflow correctly.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A number's last digit can be read directly using modulo 10, and that same digit can be removed from the number using integer division by 10, with no need to ever convert anything to a string.

Observation 2: Rebuilding the reversed number by computing result times 10 plus the new digit is the arithmetic mirror of how a positional number is written out, each step shifts everything already collected one place to the left before adding the newest digit.

Observation 3: The real difficulty here is not the reversal itself, it is that the reversed value might not fit back into a signed 32 bit integer, and that overflow must be caught before it happens, not after, since in a genuinely fixed width type the value could already have silently wrapped around by the time it is checked.

Observation 4: The check result greater than INT_MAX minus digit, all divided by 10, is derived by rearranging the very operation about to be performed, result times 10 plus digit greater than INT_MAX, solved for result, so the overflow is caught before the multiplication and addition ever run.

That reframing, from string reversal to arithmetic peeling, and from checking overflow after the fact to preventing it before the fact, is what turns a simple looking problem into a genuine test of numeric safety.

Record the sign of the number separately, convert its absolute value to a string, reverse that string, and parse it back into a number. Reapply the sign, then check whether the result still fits inside the signed 32 bit integer range.

items: Note whether the original number was negative, and take its absolute value.
Convert that absolute value to a string and reverse the string.
Parse the reversed string back into a number.
Reapply the original sign.
If the result falls outside the signed 32 bit integer range, return 0, otherwise return the result.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: convert to a string, reverse it, parse it back, then check the range

codes.python:
INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1
INT_MIN = -2**31

def reverse(x):
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    digits = str(abs(x))[::-1]                   # convert to a string and reverse it
    reversed_x = sign * int(digits)                 # parse back into a number, reapply the sign
    if reversed_x < INT_MIN or reversed_x > INT_MAX:
        return 0                                     # outside the signed 32 bit integer range
    return reversed_x


if __name__ == "__main__":
    x = 123
    print(reverse(x))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The sign is stripped off and recorded before any string work happens, so the digit reversal only ever has to deal with a plain, non negative sequence of digits.
The parsed result is stored in a wider type than the original 32 bit integer, since the reversed value could temporarily exceed the 32 bit range before the final check rejects it.
The range check happens only once, at the very end, after the full reversed value already exists, since this version has a wider type available to safely hold that intermediate value.

blocks.text: This is correct, since reversing the string representation of a number produces exactly the same digits in reverse order, and the final range check correctly rejects anything too large or too small.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log x), proportional to the number of digits in x.
Space: O(log x), for the string built to hold and reverse the digits.

Limitation: converting the number to a string and back is not strictly necessary, the digits can be peeled off and reassembled directly using ordinary arithmetic, avoiding the extra string entirely. Doing this also requires checking for overflow one digit at a time, since in a fixed width integer type, the overflow could otherwise happen silently before it can even be detected.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the string based version works but is wasteful: it allocates a string purely to reverse the order of digits, when modulo and division can read and remove digits directly from the number itself.

What is genuinely different about doing this with plain, fixed width arithmetic: there is no wider type to safely hold an intermediate overflow, so the overflow must be predicted and caught before the operation that would cause it, not detected afterward.

Can the range check be done in advance: yes, by rearranging the multiply-and-add step algebraically, the maximum safe value of result before adding one more digit can be computed directly.

Can digit extraction and result construction happen without ever building a string: yes, modulo 10 reads the last digit and integer division by 10 removes it, while result times 10 plus digit rebuilds the number one digit at a time.

The core idea: peel digits off with modulo and division, check the overflow condition before every single multiply-and-add step, and build the result directly with no string ever created.

Peel off the last digit of the number using modulo 10, and remove it from the number using integer division by 10. Build the reversed result by shifting it left one decimal place and adding in the new digit, checking before every single addition whether doing so would push the result past the maximum allowed value.
Peel off digits one at a time using modulo and division, checking the overflow condition before every step, and rebuild the result directly with pure arithmetic.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: peel off one digit at a time, checking for overflow before building the result

codes.python:
INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1
INT_MIN = -2**31

def reverse(x):
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    x = abs(x)
    result = 0
    while x != 0:
        digit = x % 10                              # peel off the last digit
        x //= 10                                     # drop that digit from the remaining number
        if result > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10:
            return 0                                    # this digit would push the result out of range
        result = result * 10 + digit                  # shift the result left and add the new digit
    return sign * result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    x = 123
    print(reverse(x))

blocks.text: This works because modulo 10 always isolates exactly the last digit of a positive integer, and integer division by 10 always removes exactly that same digit, so the entire number is consumed one digit at a time with nothing lost or duplicated. Rebuilding via result times 10 plus digit reconstructs the reversed number in exactly the order the digits were peeled off, and checking result greater than INT_MAX minus digit, divided by 10, before that multiply-and-add step guarantees the overflow is caught before it can ever actually occur.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log x), the same order as the brute force, since every digit is still visited exactly once.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built, this is the real floor for this problem, since every digit must be examined at least once but no extra memory beyond a few variables is ever needed.

blocks.text: Whenever a problem can be solved by converting to a string, it is worth checking whether the same digit by digit logic can be done with plain arithmetic instead, using modulo to read a digit and integer division to remove it. The overflow check here is just as important as the reversal itself, and must happen before the risky operation, not after.

items: Checking for overflow only after multiplying and adding, in a fixed width integer type this can already have silently wrapped around by then.
Forgetting to handle the negative sign separately before working with the digits.
Not considering that a valid looking reversed number can still be far too large to fit in a signed 32 bit integer.

blocks.text: Explicitly asking whether the environment uses fixed width integers, and proactively mentioning the overflow check before it is asked about, shows an understanding that this problem is really about safe arithmetic, not just digit manipulation.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid converting to a string", think: peel digits with modulo 10 and integer division by 10.
If the interviewer says "what if the environment only has fixed width integers", think: check the overflow condition before the multiply-and-add step, by rearranging the operation algebraically.
If the interviewer says "what should overflow return", think: this problem specifically defines that as 0, always confirm the expected sentinel value with the interviewer.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both the string based approach and the arithmetic approach run in O(log x) time, proportional to the number of digits. The string based version needs O(log x) extra space for the string, while the arithmetic version needs only O(1) extra space, the real floor for this problem.

items: Pattern: digit by digit arithmetic manipulation using modulo and integer division, paired with a proactive overflow check performed before the risky operation, not after.

Core Idea: peel off digits with modulo 10 and integer division by 10, rebuild the reversed value with result times 10 plus digit, and check the algebraically rearranged overflow condition before every single multiply-and-add step.
Time: O(log x) for both the brute force and the optimized version, proportional to the number of digits.
Space: O(log x) for the brute force, to hold the digit string; O(1) extra for the optimized arithmetic version.
Most Important Observation: in a fixed width integer type, overflow must be predicted and prevented before an operation runs, not detected after it has already silently occurred.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the string based version; deriving and applying the pre-emptive overflow check correctly is what shows real understanding of numeric safety.
One line memory trick: peel with modulo and division, rebuild with times 10 plus digit, check overflow before, not after.
